technical: The headline startup cost is presented as the agent's cost, but it was measured under heavy CPU contention. An 11 s baseline for a two-endpoint Spring Boot app, two JVMs restarting at once on a burstable 2-vCPU node shared with Postgres and the Collector, and 100m CPU requests all inflate the agent's startup work, which is CPU-bound. Readers will copy 18 s into their probes. Fix: Change one setting and rerun the startup step. Either stagger the restarts (inventory, then orders) or raise the CPU request to 1000m, and report added startup in both conditions so readers can see how it scales with CPU. Until then, put the condition in the opening sentence and lead with the ratio, e.g. '11 s to 29 s on a CPU-tight node'.

editorial: The title's number is ambiguous and falsely precise. 'At Startup' reads as total startup time, not added time, and 17.99 comes from the median of 3 samples whose ranges spread over about 2 s. Fix: Retitle along the lines of 'The OpenTelemetry Java Agent in Splunk APM: +18 s Startup, +100 MiB, Under 1 ms at p95 (One Spring Boot Lab)'. That marks the figures as added cost, rounds them, and uses the term readers search for.

technical: The p95 change comes from a single 60-second measured window per side, with no A/A baseline, yet the post calls it 'just 0.57 ms' and builds its main story on 'each request stayed close'. Fix: Run the no-agent load twice (or three times on each side) to get a noise floor, and report p50 and p95 with their spread. If the spread is near 0.57 ms, say the p95 change was within run-to-run noise rather than quoting it to two decimals.

technical: The brief promised JVM and HTTP metrics. The post reports none of the HTTP ones and puts the 19-name count down to what the agent produced, although the lookup (agent_names in fix.sh) may have missed them. The 'what you get' inventory is half of the article's promise. Fix: Query Splunk directly for the HTTP server duration histogram, filtered by sf_service:orders. Then reconcile against the names the agent printed in check.sh's console-exporter run (c/metrics.txt). Either report the HTTP metrics found, or label 19 as 'names this query returned' and explain the gap.

editorial: The trace output prints a 'null' in every row, and the text has to explain it away. It doesn't look like a real, careful session. Fix: Fix the jq path to print the field the API actually returns (span kind from tags, or duration), or drop the column and show service and operation only.

editorial: The opening points to the older issue's 61.4 s to 84.9 s and says 'so I measured it on the current one', implying a comparison. The post never makes it, and the relative overhead here is larger (+162% against +38%). Fix: Either put both relative figures side by side and say the environments differ too much to compare them, or reword the motivation so it doesn't suggest a version-over-version result.
outside claim without a known source: Maintainers have a startup PR in review reporting a 5.19% cut in agent-added startup on their benchmark
outside claim without a known source: The JVM picks up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS when it starts

Good controls: the same jar (hash shown), the same image and Collector in both runs, a before-check backed by 2098 cluster series, and a trace ID chosen by the load generator so one exact request can be fetched from Splunk.

The startup cost was measured on a CPU-starved node. A trivial Spring Boot app took 11 s to start without the agent, and both JVMs restarted together on a burstable 2-vCPU t3.large alongside Postgres and the Collector. The 17.99 s figure mostly describes that node, but the post treats it as the agent's cost.
The p95 change of 0.57 ms comes from one load run on each side, with no noise floor. 'Just 0.57 ms' and 'each request stayed close' claim more than that supports.

The count of 19 metric names, with no http.* names, may come from the query rather than from what reached Splunk. The agent's HTTP server duration histogram was never checked directly, and check.sh's console output was not used to cross-check the list.
Clear reader and a useful finding: the agent's cost shows up at startup and memory, not per request. The planning advice on startup probes and memory outside -Xmx is something a reader can act on.
The title's '17.99 Seconds at Startup' reads as total startup time, not added time, and two decimals from 3 samples is false precision.
Opens a comparison with issue 8629 (+38% on older agents), then drops it, even though this lab's relative overhead (+162%) is larger.
Partly reads as generated: the stock 'That split is the useful part', a TL;DR template, an even section rhythm, and a trace block full of 'null' that the text has to explain away.
Demand evidence is weak: a few GitHub threads (an issue with about six participants, a discussion with 11 replies, a PR) and no search or view data.
The title says 'Zero-Code Java' rather than 'OpenTelemetry Java agent', the term people with this problem would search for.
Platform engineers sizing a rollout are a real audience, but nothing linked shows how many of them want this now.

brief.reader: Platform engineer rolling out observability to Java teams on Kubernetes
brief.decision: Whether to turn on the OTel Java agent everywhere first, before asking any team for code changes
brief.question: What exactly do I get in Splunk Observability Cloud from the OTel Java agent alone, and what does it cost my service?
brief.takeaway: You can show a team its service map, traces and JVM and HTTP metrics from one environment variable, and quote measured startup, memory and p95 numbers when they ask what it costs.
brief.adds: Existing pages list what the agent can emit and how to tune overhead, and one issue reports older startup numbers. This post shows what one small Spring Boot system really produced in Splunk, and measures startup, memory and p95 on the same jar, image and Collector with the current agent.
brief.open_question: With one environment variable and no code change, how many services, metric names and spans per request does the OTel Java agent put in Splunk Observability Cloud, and how much startup time, memory and p95 latency does it add to a Spring Boot service?
tradeoffs: Agent on every service first, or hand-written instrumentation later
Default settings, or tuning instrumentation and sampling for lower overhead
Traces and metrics reach Observability Cloud here; application logs follow a separate route

A 2024 discussion with 11 replies asks about high CPU during startup, and a maintainer advises estimating overhead and reserving resources. PR 21033, ready for review since 29 Oct 2026, reports a 5.19% cut in agent-added startup. No search volume data was available.
